I didn’t hire our first marketer until we hit $6M ARR.


I waited until the business made sense.

At $0-$5M ARR, I didn’t need a marketer.
I needed to prove the business.
Who buys, why they buy, and how to repeat it.

By $6M, we had:
- inbound that worked
- a repeatable sales motion
- a clear sense of who we were and weren’t for

A setup someone could actually win in.

Then came the hard part…actually finding our marketer.

I thought I knew what I wanted.
Generalist.
Startup experience.
Not their first rodeo.

Oh, and marketing titles are a mess. The same word means 10 different things at 10 different companies.

So I just started taking calls, and a pattern showed up.

A few things I’d tell my past self:

1/ you will need to talk to a LOT of marketers. you don’t know what the market looks like yet. you need volume to calibrate “good.”

2/ most people won’t be a fit for your role. just like how most companies don’t want to buy from an early stage company, most candidates won’t want to work at an early stage company. don’t be surprised by that.

3/ you’re the market expert. they’re the execution expert. find someone who can learn the market while taking what you know and build on it.

Don’t hire a marketer to figure out your business.
Hire one to scale what you already know works.

Pick a signal that tells you about value, not the residue of decisions you made last year.

content:
I’m tired of people oversimplifying enterprise sales. Here’s every step of a $1.3M deal that took 369 days to close.

day 1: they signed up self-serve.
day 2: we got on a call. Agreed to a PoC.
day 9: check-in call. Things are going well.
day 15: ghosted.
day 22: ghosted.
day 33: hard no. 
day 34: have a post-mortem call with our champion. Ask where it fell apart. Ask what we could have done differently. Write everything down.


day 184: run into previous champion at a investor happy hour. She introduces us to a new contact at the company. We find out the problem still hasn’t been solved. A formal follow-up meeting is set.

day 195: we’re introduced to the engineering team and testing commences.
day 210: in parallel, introductions to executive, product, and engineering teams begin. they evaluate two things: company viability and business continuity.

day 211: account map created.
day 215: flew out to meet CTO in-person.

day 241: security looped in. Technical requirements discussions begin.
day 258: account map torn up. New champion identified.
day 271: technical requirements confirmed.

day 280: legal and compliance looped in. Executive meetings continue. Back-channel conversations continue.
day 295: account map rebuilt.

day 301: technical requirements changes. Meeting with engineering leadership to remap everything we’d agreed on.
day 302: commercial model changes with it.

day 310: pricing negotiations begin. Back channel to executives continue.
day 340: price finalized.
day 363: legal finalized.

day 369: signed.

The only reason this deal closed is because on day 34, when it was dead, we asked what went wrong. Everything after that came from that one call.

The messaging that got us to $10M ARR is not enough anymore.


For years, our messaging was built for a specific buyer.

”The API for developers to get transcripts, recordings, and metadata from Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet, Webex, and in-person meetings.”

Someone who’d already tried to build meeting recording themselves.
They knew how hard it was. They were looking for exactly what we do.

All I had to say was “we handle the hard parts” and they got it.
That messaging got us our first $10M.

The next stage of growth means reaching people earlier.
Before they tried to build it.

When I talk to those buyers the way I used to, their eyes glaze over.
”I don’t get why we need this. What does this actually do for us?”

That’s our messaging assuming context the buyer doesn’t have yet.

The old messaging explained how.
The new messaging has to explain why.

- when we have an FAQ comprehensive enough to build a repeatable sales playbook

content:
After closing seven $1M+ deals, I finally understand what it means to “speak the language” of C-suite.


Early on, I treated discovery with execs like I always did.
I’d ask blunt questions like:
“What’s the budget?”
“What are you trying to accomplish?”

I realized that for an executive, that’s an expensive meeting.
You’re asking them to do the work of educating you.

The higher you go, the more you have to stop acting like a vendor
and start communicating like a high-performing direct report.

Here’s what I’ve learned:

1/ change the language of the ask.

Direct questions can feel like a trap, and leave no room.
If an exec isn’t ready to share, you’ll only get a “no”.

Instead of: “What is your target price?”

Use: “You mentioned margin is a concern. Usually, that implies a specific target price. Would you be open to sharing how you arrived at that number so I can see if we’re even in the same ballpark?”

When you ask for the logic rather than price, you’re talking about their business problem.
It keeps the exec in control while your provide the path.

-----

2/ come with a hypothesis.

Don’t ask “How can we help?”
That’s a homework assignment.

Instead, show you’ve done the pre-work: “From the outside, it looks like you may be prioritizing [Y] to stay ahead of the shift toward [Industry Trend]. Am I totally off base?”

It is much easier for an exec to confirm or deny a point of view than to build one for you from scratch.

It earns you the right to their time.

-----

3/ provide the context for the follow-up.

Execs are doing a million things a minute.
Provide a contextual reminder for why the task matters.

“I know you have many competing priorities. Your deadline for solving [Problem] was [Date]. To stay on track for that, we need [Ask].”

By tying the ask to their specific problem and deadline, you’re a tool for their success.
I’ve found execs appreciate the reminder because you’ve done the work of remembering why this is important for them.

-----

An executive’s most expensive resource is their own focus.

If you’re asking them to educate you, you’re an expense.
If you’re owning the execution for them, you’re an asset.

1/ every decision must have a clearly decided decision maker
2/ the decision maker is always a person, never a department or group
3/ the decision maker is the person who has the most context on the decision, not the most seniority

We do this because consensus is a hiding place.

Most people are uncomfortable being the only one to make a call. 
They revert to consensus because if everyone agrees, no one is to blame when things break. 

But consensus is designed to avoid risk, not to find the right answer. 
It produces the worst results.

This model is only possible with A-players.

You have to trust your team's decisions completely. 
If you don't trust them to be the sole decision maker, you shouldn't have hired them.

Not eventually.
Not hypothetically.

Immediately.

This wasn’t a small optimization or a local decision
It affected the entire company.

Everyone feels it at once.

You worry about the obvious things:
- What if it fails?
- What if people lose confidence?
- What if teams feel like they’re paying the price for a bad call?

And you worry abut the less obvious ones:
- What signal does this send internally?
- What precedent does it set?
- What happens if the numbers dip before the upside shows up?

In our case, the tradeoff was clear.

Short-term revenue would go down.
Long-term velocity, leverage, and customer access would go up.

There’s no committee for bets like this.
No vote.
No A/B test.

At a certain level, leadership is about owning the blast radius.

That’s the part of leadership most people never see.

“You’re here to replace me.” The lead engineer’s voice was shaking.
Two weeks later, he pushed our $800K deal through.

Every sales call was a fight.

“Our current system already does this.”
“We don’t need another platform.”

I offered customer intros.
I tried logic.

So on a 1:1 call, I finally asked him:
“Why are you so against this?”

Long pause.

“You’re here to replace me.”

That’s when it clicked.
I was calling his baby ugly.

I was asking him to rip out months of his work.
To admit his system didn’t matter anymore.

I was trying to solve an emotional problem with a logical solution.
On the next call, I reframed the deal to make him the hero.

Instead of talking about what our product would replace,
I focused on what he would unlock.

He’d ship the new infrastructure in 2 weeks,
Get credit when it launches,
And finally get to spend time on interesting problems instead of babysitting plumbing.

Suddenly, the same engineer who was shutting us down
Became the one pulling the deal through procurement.

2 weeks later, I closed for $800K.

Most “hostile” stakeholders aren’t anti-you.

If you make their win obvious,
They’ll do more for the deal than you ever could.

One thing jumped out:
they had explicitly committed to improving reliability as a top company priority.

In the next call, I honed in on how we can help with that.

Suddenly, we were tied to something leadership had already promised the market.

-----

The goal of all this is nuance.
You’re trying to speak their language.

content:
As a co-founder of a $250M startup, here’s how I get direct reports to own things outside of their job description.

First, a misconception.

Most people don’t avoid ownership.
They avoid owning things that feel optional.

That’s a communication and hiring problem.

Here’s how I address that:

1/ Make ownership explicit by tying it to consequence

When I want someone to own a project,
I don’t assume they understand why it matters. 

I make the expectation and the consequence clear.

For example, I’ll say: 
“This is a top priority.
This came directly from a customer who’s blocked on it.
If we don’t solve this, we risk losing them.”

That does two things at once:
- it clarifies why the work matters
- it sets expectations

-----

2/ Hire for people who optimize for impact

Some candidates are drawn to the work itself.
A specific programming language.
A tool.
A narrow type of work they enjoy.

Others care about impact.
It’s less about the how, more about
what are we doing, and why are we doing it.

In interviews, I listen for the difference.

When someone describes their past work, I’ll ask:
- “Why did you choose to do that?”
- “Why did that matter to the business?”
- “What changed because of it?”

People who are impact-driven can explain:
- the business reason behind the work
- the tradeoffs they made
- the outcome they were responsible for

Impact-driven people are the ones who adapt when the job keeps changing.

-----

Startups don’t stay static long enough for rigid roles.

To manage through constant change,
you have to make outcomes explicit and hire people who can own them.

The expensive habit I had to unlearn managing a $250M company:
answering my team’s questions too quickly.

Before, these conversations were automatic.
Direct report: “Hey, I’m having trouble with this.”
Me: “Okay, then do X, Y, Z.”

But as the company grew, so did the problems.
Scopes got larger.
Situations got more nuanced.
The people asking often had teams of their own.

Every time I jumped in, 
I’d have to reconstruct context I didn’t fully have,
solve a problem I wasn’t closest to,
and walk away thinking: “that’s another thing on my plate.”

Now, when a direct report brings me a problem, 
I don’t respond with a solution.

I ask one question:
“What’s your plan?”

That does three things immediately:
- it keeps ownership with them
- it gives them the opportunity to figure it out 
- it lets me evaluate their abilities

I can still give feedback.
I can still pressure-test the plan. 
But I’m no longer carrying the problem for them. 

Teaching judgement takes more patience upfront.
But solving everyone’s problems costs you time and hides where your team actually needs to grow.

I landed six $1M deals last year. Here’s when/how I rescue 7 figure deals by flying to prospects: 

For context:
Recall.ai is the API for meeting recording on every platform like Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Webex, Slack Huddles, and in-person.

We're used by companies like HubSpot, ClickUp, and Metaview to get real-time recordings, transcripts, and speaker data into their products.

I fly out when a deal hits a roadblock,
and I don’t know why.

This is the playbook:

1/ Make it easy to say yes

I never ask:
“Can I fly out to meet you?” 

Instead, I’m specific: 
“I’m going to be in Atlanta on Friday from 2-7pm. 
Could we connect for dinner?”

Why this works:
- it signals effort without desperation
- a tight time window is easier to say yes to
- it reduces coordination work for a busy exec

-----

2/  Fly out to uncover, not to pitch

In one deal, I learned that a decision maker was about to say no. 

That surprised me.
On Zoom, she never raised an objection.

I flew out to meet her,
and that’s when she told me the truth: 
she was more committed to her internal solution than I realized.

That information let me walk through:
- the edge cases she hadn’t considered
- the ceiling she’d hit
- the tradeoffs she was about to own

Why this works:
- you’re meeting them on their turf
- you have the exec’s full attention
- they don’t need to perform in front of their team

-----

3/ Be picky about where you meet

The setting determines the conversation you get. 

If I need to meet with multiple stakeholders,
I meet at their office.

It’s easier to loop people in
and align everyone at once.

If I need one exec’s honest take,
I meet outside HQ.

Why this works:
- offices optimize for alignment
- out-of-office settings optimize for candor
- the room shapes what people feel safe saying

-----

Flying out isn’t just about pushing the deal forward.
It’s about finding out what’s actually blocking it.

Seed tests momentum.
Series A tests trust.
Series B tests vision.

I’ve done over 500 founder-led sales calls. These are the 4 things I wish I knew earlier:

1/ Always talk less than the prospect.
Aim for 40% talk time.
Listening forces you to hear the real problem, not just the one you assumed.

2/ Never interrupt.
Not even with “mhm,” “okay,” or “yep.”
Let them get every thought out before you speak.
Show you’re listening with your face, not your mouth.

3/ Qualify hard.
This alone cut our sales cycle in half.
In discovery, we tell prospects every option on the market,
including how they could build in-house.
It builds trust, and it pushes unqualified deals out early.

4/ Stop demo-ing everything.
Our demos are 10 minutes,
Tailored only to their use case.
When you show less, the prospects naturally ask more questions.
Now they’re leading the demo and giving you more signal on what they care about.

Lesson: visibility is half the product.

In my head, the vision couldn’t be clearer.

Lesson: over-communicate until people start quoting you.

Not because we had SOC2.
Not because we looked like an enterprise vendor.
But because one senior leader said, “I’ll take the hit if this goes wrong.”

What I didn’t understand at the time was that they already liked our product, and were evaluating the risk of working with us.

Could we support them?
Will we be alive in two years?
Would choosing us blow back on them?

And the wild part is that none of these questions get answered in one meeting.

Mid-market = 1 person making a decision.
Enterprise = 15-50 people trying to agree on anything.

Half the calls I had with them were their own teams catching each other up.

I wasn’t selling.
I was project managing a group that didn’t work for me.

Our first enterprise deal actually died twice.
Both times, our champion dragged it back to life.

That was the moment I finally understood who actually closes these deals.

Not the founder.
Not the AE.
The person inside who’s willing to risk their reputation on you.

Funny thing is… every founder I know has a completely different story about how their first enterprise deal actually closed.

I sent a $1.2M contract way too early. Their CTO shut the deal down on the spot, and that’s what saved it.

The VP of Engineering was excited and wanted to move fast.

No demo.
No deep-dive.

His team validated the technical fit in a day and told him, “We can run this in production.”

So after the disco call, we kicked off everything in parallel:
- Security
- Procurement
- Legal
- Commercials

Five separate threads. 
None of them talking to each other.

On Day 5, the VP asked for the contract.
I sent it.

Two hours later, the CTO rejected the contract and replied:
“Do not move forward.”

The email exposed the problem:

Finance hadn’t synced with Eng team.
The CTO had no context at all.

The urgency was still there, but the contract exposed the lack of alignment.

It forced every stakeholder to raise their hand.
It gave us the full buying committee in one shot.

Once everyone surfaced, the work was straightforward:
security review, pricing, fallback plan, legal terms, technical requirements.

The contract kicked off what I should have done from the start.
Coordinate.

The deal closed on Day 47.

In enterprise sales, a “no” isn’t a rejection.
It’s the moment the deal finally starts.

a competitor, a Google search trend, an addressable TAM.

There were plenty of note-taking tools.
Prospects showed interest.

But the deeper I went –
wiring together integrations, processing audio data, handling timestamps–
the more cracks I started to see.

The real problem wasn’t notetaking.
It was the layer underneath: recording the meetings across platforms, maintaining bots, retrieving transcripts.

You only notice those kinds of things once you’ve lived inside the problem long enough to feel its limits.

From the outside, most things look solid.
But when you zoom in, you see how everything’s just a set of moving parts, barely holding together.

That’s where new companies are born:
in the gaps that only appear once you’re close enough to see them.

The key to a successful startup isn’t solving a problem everyone already knows.
It’s solving one no one’s noticed yet.

The hardest part wasn’t writing the email.

“Who needs this now?”

Not “who might be interested.”

- “Companies hiring {ICP role}”

- Lusha

But it all still comes down to the same thing:

If you don’t know who needs your product, no tool will save you.
If you do know, even Google Search is enough.

The list is everything. The outreach is just execution.

content:
The goal of sales is not to convince someone to buy.


I used to treat discovery calls like a game I had to win.
Nail the pitch. Smash objections. Get to yes.
Somewhere along the way, I forgot why I started doing founder-led sales in the first place.

It wasn't to close deals.
It was to help people solve real problems.

Early on at Recall, I'd spend 30 minutes walking through features, anticipating questions, trying to prove we were the right choice.
But I was treating prospects like targets, not people.

The shift happened when I stopped opening with a pitch and started opening with a question:

“What made you take this call?”

Not just because I wanted to shorten sales cycles
But because I wanted to re-humanize them.

When a prospect says: “Leadership wants to ship new features but engineering is buried in meeting integration maintenance”
I know exactly how to help.

When someone says: “Just exploring options”,
I know they're not ready yet, and that's okay.
We'll talk again when they are.

When you start with curiosity instead of persuasion, people stop performing and start sharing.

That’s what founder-led sales is supposed to be.
Humans helping humans.

Closed my 5th seven-figure deal last month. Finally saw the playbook everyone says doesn’t exist.

Yes, there’s no script, formula, or guaranteed sequencing for enterprise deals.
But there is a scaffold.

Every seven-figure deal eventually hits the same checkpoints:
First meeting → demo → technical validation → PoC → PoC sign-off → procurement → security → legal → contract.

But the real work isn’t the checklist.
It’s what you do when you’re stuck between checkpoints.

For context:
Recall.ai is the API for meeting recording on every platform like Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Webex, Slack Huddles, and in-person.

We're used by companies like HubSpot, ClickUp, and Metaview to get real-time recordings, transcripts, and speaker data into their products.

Here are the things that have actually moved our seven-figure deals forward:

- Backchanneling to learn who’s worried, who’s confused, and who’s blocking silently
- Flying out when a senior stakeholder joins late and wants to “reassess”
- Hosting a small dinner to align teams who weren’t looped in until mid-PoC
- Getting warm intros from investors or any mutual connections
- Running security + procurement in parallel so they don’t choke the timeline later
- Showing up early to events stakeholders are speaking at
- Going backwards a checkpoint when something collapses, instead of forcing the next step

None of these moves look like “selling.”
None of them follow a proper sequence.

That’s why people say there’s no playbook.
But there is a framework and checkpoints you have to hit.

What’s the most creative thing you’ve done to get to the next checkpoint?

But I didn’t understand the milestones I had to hit on the way there,
which made every call awkward.

Here’s the core insight:
Discovery → Demo → Trial → Close.
This is the simplest version of a sales process framework.

The goal of discovery is simple: if the prospect is qualified, the next step is to get them on a demo.

In discovery, you want to understand them deeply: use case, timeline, constraints, and decision criteria.
In the demo, they start to understand your solution more deeply.

Once I shifted my disco call goal from “sign the contract” to “book the demo inside the call,”
Everything clicked.

In sales, the goal of every meeting is to book the next one.

content:
I’ve closed 6 $1M+ deals. This is how I revive a deal when I’m hit with a no.

For context:
Recall.ai is the API for meeting recording on every platform like Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Webex, Slack Huddles, and in-person.

We're used by companies like HubSpot, ClickUp, and Metaview to get real-time recordings, transcripts, and speaker data into their products.

When a deal stalls mid-flight, I don’t push harder.
I rewind the deal to the last checkpoint where everyone was aligned.

Here are some common ones:
1/ Technical validation
“We need X and you don’t have it.” 
This is almost never about the feature.

It’s about understanding the question behind the question:
“What is the reason you need X?”

If you understand the constraint behind the requirement,
you can offer a better solution that solves their exact problem. 

-----

2/ Financial validation
“Your pricing is too high”

How I respond:
- “Compared to what?”
- “What budget is this actually coming from?”
- “What is cost of doing nothing?”

If the champion can’t answer those,
you have a discovery gap. 

-----

3/ Risk validation
“It doesn’t match X security requirement”
“We can’t accept this clause”

What’s consistently worked for me:
get everyone who is concerned on a call.

Live conversations surface:
- missing context
- incorrect assumptions
- what actually needs to change

Vague risk objections don’t survive real-time discussion.

-----

A “no” in enterprise sales isn’t a rejection.
It’s a signal you’re missing context.

99% of my time is spent fielding no’s. But this “no” killed a $1M deal, and I needed to know why. 

Two days after the “no”, I found out they had a booth at a conference.
And one of the DM’s would be there.

So I showed up 30 minutes early on Day 1.
Not with a deck or a pitch. 
Just questions.

On a high-top table at 7:30AM, I got a chance to talk 1-1, 
and that’s when the real “no” surfaced. 

I asked how she was thinking about the decision. 
Not the group, not the process, just her perspective.

She finally shared what was on her mind:
- who would be on the hook if this failed
- how this decision would look six months later if priorities shifted
- whether buying now would box them into something they couldn’t unwind quietly

None of that came up in the first meeting. 

While that 30 minute conversation didn’t close the deal…
It reopened it. 

She pulled us back into the process, and this time, she was the one pushing it forward.

In enterprise sales, sometimes the way to get to the truth is to:
change the room, 
change the conversation, 
or show up early enough to be a human.

- “Tell me about a time you disagreed with him.”

Was it always the product? The market? Other people?

At this stage, I still want a VP of Sales who can sell (not just talk about selling).

There was always a take-home.
I had candidates sell to us and put together a sales plan.

This is someone I need to trust to act in the company’s best interest.

A lot of candidates didn’t make it through this process.

Selling into 10,000+ employee companies taught me that the closer a deal gets to yes, the more people will say no.

Early in our enterprise deals, I used to read this as a bad sign.

More objections.
More stakeholders.
More “concerns” popping up from people we haven’t talked with at seemingly random points.

After enough enterprise deals, I started seeing it differently.

Once a deal looks real, people start coming out of the woodwork.
Not to block it but to be attached to it.

If they’re climbing the ladder inside a large org, being part of an important evaluation is career-positive.
And the easiest way to “add value” in that moment is to say no.

The way to handle these “no’s” is by:
- getting them into 1-on-1s
- hearing them out individually
- asking for their perspective
- addressing their concerns directly

This is an opportunity to get more information.

And to be honest, this is a good sign. Deals that aren’t going anywhere don’t attract this behavior.
The more people surface concerns, the more important the deal had become internally.

content:
Traffic grew 20x in the last 18 months. Here’s a breakdown of how that actually happened.

This wasn’t one channel.
And it definitely wasn’t a single spike.

It was a few things compounding at different moments.

-----

December 2024: LinkedIn 

I started taking LinkedIn seriously. Started posting what I wished I’d known earlier and what I was actively learning while building.

The early posts didn’t do much. Then a few started landing. Then I got better at writing. Then the audience started to grow. 

When I look at referral traffic from LinkedIn, it follows the same curve as our overall sit traffic: slow at first, then compounding.

-----

Early 2025: Engineering content

Two engineering blog posts hit the top of Hacker News. They were deeply technical posts about the problems we run into building the foundational infrastructure for the world’s largest dataset. 

The blogs spread far beyond HN: Slack groups, international newsletters, and even back onto LinkedIn. Those blog posts still come up in conversations months later.

-----

September 2025: Series B

The Series B campaign didn’t spike traffic the way earlier moments did, but conversion changed noticeably. People who had been following quietly started reaching out. Evaluations that had been slow suddenly picked up. By then, there was enough proof in the market: the Desktop Recording SDK was live, and notable customers were already running products on top of our API.

-----

If there’s a pattern here, it’s:
- show up where your actual audience already pays attention
- publish things that are hard to fake
- and let credibility compound over time.

Growth doesn’t feel dramatic while it’s happening. It only looks obvious in hindsight.

Today, running a $250M company, I have 60 minute 1-1s with every person in our GTM team. This is why this works.

As the company scaled, I was tempted to compress 1-1s, but I found 30 minutes to be too short for anything real to surface.

- the complex problem they’ve been stuck on but can’t articulate yet
- the thing they “don’t want to bother you with”
- the early signs of misalignment that only show up in long-form conversation

And once you hear those things through, 90% of the time, the solution becomes obvious because your direct report finally had room to talk through it.

The hour matters because:
- trust takes time to reveal itself
- sometimes the problem is unclear until it is said out loud
- a single good conversation can make the next two weeks dramatically more productive

It’s also a very inexpensive and effective use of the hour.
One hour every two weeks prevents months of misalignment.

The only reason I know this is because I started to skip them.
And I felt the disconnect immediately.
Problems started to compound.

This has been the highest-ROI GTM habit I’ve kept.
Even at this stage.

1/ Don’t start with a strategy. Start with reps.
I didn’t have a plan, pillars, or themes.
I just posted every day to get as many at-bats as possible.
If a post/comment doesn’t do well, no one will see it anyway.

2/ Write what you’d actually read.
If you wouldn’t stop scrolling for it, no one else will.
Start by asking: what value can I provide?
What answers, examples, or shortcuts could make someone’s tomorrow easier?
Every great post/comment starts with what you’d want to learn.

3/ Find your repeatable hits.
After a month, patterns emerge.
I found myself gravitating towards certain topics, and those were the ones getting results.
Double down on what compounds.
That’s when I started building out content pillars.

4/ Constantly test.

content:
You may have heard we raised our $38M Series B. It was the fastest and smoothest round we’ve done. Here’s what worked and what I’d do differently.

1/ Build relationships before you’re fundraising

Every founder hears “build relationships early,” but here’s why it matters:

Series B investors make a few bets a year.
They need time to understand your market, talk to your customers, and form a thesis.
If you wait until you’re officially raising, it’s already too late.

Start meeting investors months in advance.
Show them progress in real time (product milestones, customer stories, hiring updates).
When it’s time to raise, they’ll already have conviction.

-----

2/ Run a fast, parallel process

Once you kick off, speed matters more than ever.

A raise is basically an auction for your equity.
The best outcome comes when multiple bidders show up at the same time.

Set a tight window. Two weeks from first meeting to term sheet.
Share updates proactively so everyone is aligned.
The first offer you get sets the pace for everyone else.

-----

3/ Give investors time before the process, not during

You can’t make diligence faster.
You can only move it earlier.

Investors want to do their homework: talk to customers, competitors, and your team.
If they’ve already done that before you open the round, they can move in days, not months.

That’s why relationship-building isn’t “networking.”
It’s pre-work for a fast process.

-----

4/ Treat Series B like an early-stage round

What surprised us most: Series B still feels early stage.

Investors still cared 90% about the vision and how this becomes a massive company.
Numbers prove progress.
Story sells the future.
Don’t forget to lead with WHY this can be big.

-----

5/ Prep your materials before you start

We had everything ready:

- A tight deck (see here: https://lnkd.in/dVm8uFZq)
- Customer references on standby
- FAQs with clear answers investors could reuse internally

You won’t have time to scramble.

-----

What I’d do differently next time:

Start the relationship-building even earlier.
Give investors more time to understand the business so when the auction starts, they’re already ready to bid.

content:
When I first started doing founder-led sales, I had no idea how to run an enterprise deal. Today we sell to dev teams at companies like HubSpot and Rippling. Here’s what I’ve learned about multi-threading early.

It’s easy to start multi-threading when deals stall.
By then, it’s too late.
You need to build internal alignment before the first call.

Here’s what I do:

Phase 1: Before the meeting

1/ Research the invite list
Look at everyone on the calendar.
Understand their role, team, and what “success” likely means for them.

2/ Connect early
Send short, personal LinkedIn messages to everyone attending.
“Hey [Name], noticed you’ll be joining the meeting on [date]. Looking forward to understanding your perspective.”

You’d be surprised how many people click through your profile before the call.

3/ Send a single-threaded pre-meeting email to every attendee
“Hi [Name], I see you’ll be part of our discussion next week. [Main POC] has been super helpful so far, and I’d love to make sure we address everyone’s needs. What aspects of [solution/product] would be most valuable for you?”
One reply from a secondary stakeholder can completely change how you frame the call.

------

Phase 2: During the meeting

4/ Start by aligning goals
“What specific outcome of today’s meeting would make this meeting valuable for you?”
You’ll surface hidden priorities.

5/ Read the room
If someone looks lost or disengaged, DM them directly:
“We may have rushed through [topic], would a quick clarification help?”
“This seems to resonate with you. Should we explore this aspect further?”
Treat the meeting like a conversation, not a presentation.

-----

Phase 3: After the meeting

6/ Follow up with every attendee in a single-threaded message with context
Re-watch the call. Look for moments where individuals leaned in or dropped off.
Then tailor your follow-ups:
“Wanted to clarify [concept] from our discussion. Here’s a short explanation.”
“You seemed excited about [topic]. Here’s a quick resource expanding on that.”
Within 24 hours, every attendee should have 1:1 message from you that feels written just for them.

------

Why this works

You’re building alignment before anyone asks for it.
By the time procurement or leadership steps in, you already have advocates across the table.

This is how you turn one conversation into multiple champions.
And that’s how early-stage founders close enterprise deals faster.

When hiring at a startup, the most important question isn’t about skills. It’s: “What do you want in life?” And ideally, they show you in how they’ve lived.

Someone who needs external validation will burn out when customers reject the first three product iterations.
Someone who wants predictable hours will resent the all-hands-on-deck moments that define startups.

“What frustrates you most about your current role?”

I’m not looking for perfect answers. I’m looking for people whose natural wiring matches our reality.
Skills can be developed. Fundamental motivations can’t be changed.
Get the incentives right, and everything else becomes easier.

content:
Every $200K+ deal we closed this year had the same 30/70 split. We talked 30%, they talked 70%. Here’s what active listening actually looks like in practice.

Earlier this year, we were losing a deal. The prospect kept saying our pricing was “too expensive” and they could “just run their own infrastructure.”

------

Here’s the actual conversation that turned it around:

Prospect: “Look, this is just too expensive. It’s cheaper to run our own infra. It works most of the time.”

Me: “Let me make sure I understand. You like Recall and want to stay with us, but the price is the blocker. And you’re unsure because your in-house build works 95% of the time, but when that 5% happens, everything’s on fire. Is that right?”

Prospect: “Exactly. And when those recordings don’t happen, our customers lose trust in us.”
Me: “So what happens during that 5% when the recordings fail?”

Prospect: “We scramble. We drop everything. Customers get angry. It’s a nightmare.”

At that point, they started selling themselves. The deal closed two weeks later.

-----

I didn’t pitch features. I didn’t counter their objections. 
I just repeated back what they told me until they heard their own problem clearly.

People won’t listen to your solution until they feel heard about their problem. Most prospects give you a jumbled monologue mixing what they want with what’s broken. Your job is to untangle it and reflect it back.

The magic happens when they say “exactly.” That’s when you know you’ve earned the right to solve their problem.

Active listening isn’t just nodding along. It’s making sure they know you understand before you try to be understood.

Mid-demo, the prospect would ask: “Okay, but how much does this cost?”
And I’d answer right then and there.

Here’s the problem:
When pricing is discussed before everyone is aligned on the value, you lose any benchmark to compare the price to.

When pricing comes up too early, don’t dodge it but park it.

Say:
”Before we move on, do you have any other product or technical questions? I want to make sure we cover everything before we talk pricing.”

Then keep looping until there’s nothing left:
“Any concerns?”
”Does this answer your question?”
“Anything missing for your team?”

This isolates objections.
Because once every product/technical question is resolved, the only thing left is price.
And at that point, you have alignment your product solves their problem.

That’s how I closed our first $100K deal and every 6-figure deal since.

OpenAI just dropped GPT-5. If you’re building with customer data, here’s the no hype playbook to use it right.

OpenAI launched a router model that automatically decides when to answer fast (cheap) vs think harder (expensive).
You don’t have to pick the model anymore.

What this means for any startup:

400K context window = analyze entire customer conversations, not fragments
Better tool-calling = your AI workflows actually work consistently
Smart cost management = cheap for simple tasks, expensive only when needed

Behind the scenes:

GPT-5 full - Best accuracy, highest cost
GPT-5 mini - 40-50% cheaper, slight quality drop
GPT-5 nano - Super fast, mobile friendly
GPT-5 thinking - Deep reasoning (slower, pricier)

-----

If you’re building with conversations (sales calls, interviews, meetings), here’s your playbook:

1/ start small: wire up gpt-5-mini with reasoning_effort=”minimal” for your default pipeline; watch token usage.

2/ burst up intelligently: detect “decision-heavy” segments (e.g. pricing talk, objections) and re-run that slice through full gpt-5 or GPT-5 thinking.

3/ refactor tool chains: replace custom retry logic with GPT-5’s native pre-/post-tool messages; early tests report ~50% fewer hard failures.

4/ RAG rethink: with 400K context you can sometimes skip the retrieval layer for short datasets (e.g. single-account sales history) and just drop the docs in-prompt

5/ cost guardrails: cap maximal tokens when pipeline runs on pro; token surges are real.

-----

What this unlocks:

1/ freemium & live-assist products can migrate to *nano/mini* for cheaper, snappier UX, while still rising to full GPT-5 intelligence when it matters.

2/ enterprise workflows get way simpler. no more chunking meetings into 20 pieces.

3/ agentic workflows (automated follow-ups, CRM updates) get sturdier thanks to better tool adherence.

content:
This demo structure won’t work for everyone. But it increased our conversion rate by 57% so steal it if you want. WARNING: dense post ahead

We used to think a great demo needed to cover everything.
That just made people zone out.

So we rebuilt our demo. Now the average one takes 15 minutes, and it outperforms every version we’ve tried.

Here’s our EXACT structure (minute by minute):

0:00 - Set the stage (reframe the demo around them, not us)

1/ Recap what they told us in discovery.
→ “So you’re looking to pull transcripts into your product from Zoom and Google Meet?”
2/ Confirm outcomes. Not features.
→ “So your goal is speed to market…does that sound right?”

Why it works: You earn permission to skip 90% of the product and go deep on the pain that matters.

-----

2:00 - Make it interactive early (get them talking before you start demoing)

1/ Ask them to name the meeting bot. Literally.
→ “Want to give your bot a name real quick?”
2/ Customize the demo with their name, brand, or use case.

Why this works: Now they’re not watching a product. They’re watching their product.

-----

4:00 - Show just enough (curiosity > coverage)

1/ Walk through 3 endpoints:
→ Create Bot
→ Get Transcript
→ Get Recording
2/ Go slow. Circle key parts. Pause often.
→ “Does this make sense?”

Why this works: By showing less, they ask more. Now they’re pulling the demo forward.

-----

10:00 - Qualify without sounding salesy (no “next steps” slide. just conversation.)

1/ Ask soft-close questions
→ “Do you have any questions on how you’d use this API?”
→ “Does it all make sense from a technical perspective what you need to do integrate?”
→ “Does it all make sense from a product perspective what the user experience will be like?”

Why this works: This surfaces objections early and builds confidence. No pitch needed.

-----

13:00 - Stop while they want more 
(end demo early. let them lead the next move.)

1/ Don’t push a timeline. Let them drive.
→ “Happy to go deeper — what’s most useful from here?”

Why it works: People are more likely to lean in when they’re not being sold to. We found they usually ask for a trial or a security doc at this point.

-----

Bonus details that really matter:
- The bot joins the call in real-time. That moment always lands.
- We preload a Postman collection but only walk through 3 endpoints. The other endpoints sit like easter eggs on the side.
- We don’t send a follow-up deck. We send the docs and let them give it a go.

If you’re demoing to prove how much you’ve built, you’ll lose.
We demo to prove how much we’ve understood.
This structure won’t work for every product, but the principles should stay the same.

Here’s what actually worked (and took the most time):

1/ Start with a seed list
I knew a handful of companies already using meeting bots. That gave me a starting point.

2/ Expand manually
I used LinkedIn and Google to find competitors, adjacent tools, and anyone selling to the same buyer. Hours of clicking that you can probably save time on now.

3/ Test every title
I didn’t know if our buyer was a CTO, Head of Product, Eng, or Developer. So I emailed all of them and watched who replied. Patterns showed up fast. Start small.

4/ Disqualify aggressively
Once I knew the right type of company and person, I only emailed people I was confident had the problem right now.

I didn’t have the best copy.
I just built the best list.
And that made all the difference.

Traction is easy. PMF is not.


At my first startup, I made the same mistake most founders do:

We had traction.
Growth looked good.
Investors were interested.

But deep down, something felt off.

People were signing up. But they weren’t sticking.

They weren’t using the product the way we thought they would.
They weren’t telling their teammates.
They weren’t asking for more.

That’s when it hit me:

Traction is just motion.
PMF is when that motion becomes inevitable.

Traction is:
- Hitting $10K MRR
- Getting 100 signups
- Growing 20% MoM

PMF is:
- People bugging you for access
- Users asking for features before you build them
- Teams reorganizing around your product

One is easy to manufacture.
The other hits like gravity.

If you’re early, don’t confuse activity for truth.
Chasing growth is tempting.
But chasing *pull* is what actually matters.

Don’t use trials to convince people to care.
Use trials to confirm the product works.

content:
Our exact qualification framework from $0-$1M ARR.


When I first started selling, I wasted months on prospects who would never buy. So I created this simple matrix to instantly sort every lead.

FAST CLOSE (High problem fit, High buying readiness)

- All calls focus on implementation
- Expedited contracts
- CEO involved in closing
- Prioritize over all other deals

EDUCATION NEEDED (Low problem fit, High buying readiness)

- Has budget and urgency
- Doesn't fully understand solution value
- Max 2 education calls
- If still unclear, DISQUALIFY

NURTURE (High problem fit, Low buying readiness)

- Perfect use case match
- Timeline >90 days or budget not approved
- Send monthly check-ins, not weekly
- No custom demos or proposals

DISQUALIFY (Low problem fit, Low buying readiness)

- Immediately disqualify

- If they ask for a trial extension, ask for a commitment to a decision date.

- If they want flexible payment terms, ask for an introduction to the economic buyer.

This does three things. It shortens the sales cycle. It strengthens the relationship. It prevents discounting away deals that would have closed anyway.

- The dilution difference between Seed and Series A is small (~20%).
- But Series A expectations are way higher. Team size, traction, and retention must be locked.

These benchmarks are baselines, not rules.

The best founders use market data to inform, not dictate, their raise.

Your growth strategy sucks... 


Word-of-mouth is an outcome, not a strategy.

Most founders think if they build a great product, people will just talk about it.

They won’t.

Word-of-mouth doesn’t just happen. You have to engineer it.

Here’s how:

1️⃣ Give people a reason to share.

Nobody shares a product just because it works. They share it because it makes them look smart, solves a painful problem, or gives them social currency. If you’re not giving them that, they won’t talk.

2️⃣ Make sharing the default.

Built-in viral loops, refer-a-friend programs, and exclusive access work for a reason. Slack didn’t go viral because it was “great.” It forced teams to onboard together, making sharing part of the product itself.

3️⃣ Talk about your product so much that others start doing it for you.

If you’re not constantly telling your own story, why would anyone else? Repeat your messaging so much others start doing it for you. Tell the same story, and remember to engage your early adopters. Amplify their feedback.

4️⃣ Find your early amplifiers.

Your first power users matter more than your first 1,000 users. Identify the people who love your product and help them spread the word. Give them tools. Give them incentives.

The best products don’t spread by accident. They spread because someone did the work to make sure they would.

Ask for a small work sample. If they can’t deliver, run. The best candidates love showing what they can do.

When raising Series A, a VC asked me a question: “How do you keep raising the hiring bar without making your team feel threatened?”

As founders, we want to hire the best.
We want every new hire to be stronger, smarter, and better than the last.

For us, that’s exciting.
For some employees, it’s uncomfortable.

A VC once asked me this:
“You and your co-founder want to hire better every time. But what about the rest of your team? Not everyone will be as comfortable with that. How do you keep raising the bar without making them feel replaceable?”

That question stuck with me.

Because early-stage hiring isn’t just about finding great people. It’s about making sure your team sees them as an addition, not a threat.

Here’s how we think about it now:

1/ Make hiring part of the culture, not a disruption.
The team should expect every new hire to raise the bar. If hiring A-players is part of your DNA, it won’t feel like a shift. It’ll feel like a win.

2/ Involve the team in hiring decisions.
People fear what they don’t control. If they’re part of the process, giving feedback, and defining what’s needed. They see new hires as teammates, not competition.

3/ Growth solves fear.
People don’t fear great hires if they know there’s more opportunity ahead. The best teams believe growth creates more chances, not fewer.

4/ A-players want A-players.
If someone resists hiring better talent, it’s usually because they’re unsure about their own place on the team. The best employees push for higher standards, not against them.

That VC’s question changed how I think about hiring.
Because hiring better isn’t just about talent. It’s about creating a team that wants to grow with it.

If your team isn’t excited about raising the bar, the real problem isn’t hiring. It’s culture.

How do you hire better without breaking company culture?

5/ Foster authentic FOMO.

Because our process was tight, investors saw others moving quickly, which created natural urgency. We didn’t need to force FOMO—it happened because we were in control.

Fundraising isn’t just about pitching. It’s about process. Treat it like a sales pipeline, and you’ll stay in control of your round.

Seed: Raise when demand is undeniable
- $100k - $300k ARR

- $1M - $3M ARR
- You have a repeatable acquisition channel
- You’ve proven retention. 80% of users/customers stay after X months

Series B+: Raise when capital = scale
- $8M+ ARR
- You can confidently say, “Every $1 we put in = at least $3 out.”
- You can see a clear path to $100M+ revenue.

My main takeaway is that the best founders raise because they’ve built leverage. Customers, revenue or growth momentum investors can’t ignore.

1️⃣ The Decision-Maker isn’t in the room
In startups, the founder decides. In enterprises, your champion is just one voice.

How to fix it:

- Backchannel early. Map out who owns the decision.
- Align with executives before procurement.
- Arm your champion. If they can’t sell it internally, the deal is already lost.

The best sales teams don’t just work the deal. They work the company.

2️⃣ Enterprises buy less risk, not more features
Startups buy fast. Enterprises buy what’s safest.

How to fix it:

- De-risk the decision. Case studies, compliance, SLAs. These aren’t optional.
- Sell the company, not just the product. They need to believe you’ll be here in 5 years.
- Make rollout easy. If it feels like work, they’ll push it off indefinitely.

Nobody gets fired for choosing IBM. Your job is to make choosing your startup feel just as safe.

3️⃣ Time kills all deals
We lost a Fortune 500 deal because security approvals took too long.

After months of back and forth, we finally got through. The next day, the budget was gone.

How to fix it:

- Move fast on things you control.
- Create urgency, but don’t rush them. Enterprises move at their own speed.
- Stay ahead of org changes. If a deal is dragging, ask: “What happens if this gets pushed to next quarter?”

Enterprise deals don’t die because of competition. They die in slow-moving pipelines.

The biggest mistakes I made making a $10M ARR company, and what I’d do differently if I started over:

Growing a company to $10M ARR teaches you a lot. Mostly, it teaches you what not to do.

Here are the biggest mistakes I made scaling to $10M ARR, and what I’d do differently:

1/ Waiting too long to hire key roles

- Early on, I tried to do too much myself. By the time I realized I needed to hire, I was stretched thin and making rushed decisions.
- What I’d do differently: Identify critical hires before they become urgent. Hire for where the company is going, not just where it is today.

2/ Chasing too many things at once

- We experimented with too many channels, features, and initiatives. The result? Half-baked execution and slower momentum.
- What I’d do differently: Pick one go-to-market motion and go deep. The fastest-growing startups aren’t doing everything—they’re doing one thing incredibly well.

3/ Not charging enough early on

- We priced based on what we thought the market expected, rather than the actual value we provided.
- What I’d do differently: Charge more, sooner. The best customers aren’t looking for the cheapest option—they’re looking for the best solution.

4/ Thinking great products sell themselves

- We assumed that if the product was good, people would talk about it. That’s not how it works.
- What I’d do differently: Engineer word-of-mouth. Build in virality, create shareable moments, and talk about the product so much that others start doing it for you.

5/ Underestimating how much clarity the team needs

- In my head, the vision was obvious. But in reality, people can’t execute on what they don’t fully understand.
- What I’d do differently: Over-communicate. Say the same things so many times that people start repeating them back to you.

Every founder learns these lessons the hard way. But if I had to do it again, I’d move faster, focus harder, and cut distractions sooner.

3 years ago, I was stuck in pivot-hell. Today, I run a multi-million ARR startup.
The biggest lesson: Building a startup is surprisingly similar to one of the fundamental algorithms in AI — Gradient Descent.

---

Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm to iteratively find the lowest point in a graph.

Imagine standing on a hill, and taking successive steps downhill until you can’t go any lower.

This is how many startup founders approach building their product. They start off with an idea, talk to a few users, build what users ask for, and repeat.

But there’s a problem with this approach.

When AI researchers apply gradient descent, a common problem is getting stuck in a local minimum — an area of the graph that’s lower than its surroundings, but far from the best possible result.

---

This exact same phenomenon happens with founders building products.

The first version of the product you build is probably fundamentally broken in several ways, and taking small steps to optimize it won’t bring you to PMF.

The only way to get out of a local minimum is to take bigger steps.

This makes taking bigger swings, making larger product changes, or pivoting the business — all strategies where you need to have deep conviction and a detailed understanding of your problem space.

---

That’s why it’s so important to build in a space you have deep knowledge of.
You can’t iterate to success if you’re only taking small steps.

We closed a $100K deal after 4 months and 12+ meetings. Every stakeholder played a specific role, and knowing these roles made all the difference. 

Here’s how to navigate each one:

1/ The Champion
Your biggest advocate internally. 
It’s critical you build an exceptional relationship with this person. 
Treat them like an extension of your team, and give them the proper support so they can influence the org internally.
If you don’t have a Champion, the deal gets 10x harder to close.

2/ The Coach
They help you navigate the internals of the org, but take a more passive role than the Champion. 
While the Champion actively sells your product internally, your Coach might not have direct sway but knows how to help you position yourself.
Don’t mistake your Coach for a Champion.

3/ The Key Decision Maker
If your product costs a meaningful amount of money, the Key Decision Maker typically has title of Director or above. 
They are very busy and delegate most decisions making to their team. 
It will be difficult to get 1:1 time with them given their schedule, but if you’re able to do it, it’s one of the quickest ways to move a deal forward. Plus, they can give you insight into what they care about.

4/ The Economic Buyer
In smaller orgs, the Economic Buyer and the Key Decision Maker can be the same person-typically the head of the department you’re selling into.
In larger orgs, they are likely different people, with the Economic Buyer being on the finance side.
They control the budget and care about ROI. This person isn’t interested in your product features.

5/ Process Folks
Think procurement, security and legal.
For these folks, they just need to check the box to proceed. 
Never steamroll them or treat them like obstacles - they hate that.
If you run into blockers, jump on 1:1 calls with them to progress the deal. Ask your Champion to help if all else fails.

Winning deals is about understanding what each role values and tailoring your approach to meet their needs.

- Multi-Token Reading: While traditional AI processes text word-by-word (“The… cat… sat”), DeepSeek reads phrases at once. It’s 2x faster while remaining 90% accurate.

- Expert Systems: Instead of activating all 1.8 trillion parameters at once, DeepSeek uses only what’s needed. 671B total parameters, but only 37B active at a time.

This is like replacing a massive one-size-fits-all AI with a team of specialized experts who are “called in” when needed.

3️⃣ The Results Are Wild

DeepSeek has achieved:

- 95% cheaper API costs

- Models that run on gaming GPUs instead of specialized data center hardware

- A GPU requirement drop from 100,000 to just 2,000

And here’s the kicker: It’s all open source. The code, the technical papers. It’s all out there for anyone to use or verify.

4️⃣ Why This Changes Everything

For years, AI has been the domain of massive tech companies with billion-dollar budgets. But with R1, the rules are changing:

- Barriers are falling. You don’t need a $1B data center to train competitive AI anymore. A few GPUs and clever engineering might do the trick.

- Startups have a shot. This levels the playing field, opening up AI innovation to smaller teams.

At Recall.ai, we’ve been watching the rapid evolution of LLMs closely, and DeepSeek validates what we’ve believed for a long time: the ecosystem is moving faster than anyone predicted.

The next wave of AI isn’t just about bigger, more expensive models. It’s about efficient, accessible, and specialized tools that will transform industries.

What’s your take on R1 and the role models like DeepSeek will play in reshaping AI?

Your LinkedIn posts are failing because of these 5 mistakes...


Most LinkedIn posts don’t fail because the content is bad. They fail because no one stops to read them.

Here’s why your posts might not be getting engagement—and how to fix them.

1. Your hook is weak

The first line is everything. If it doesn’t make people stop scrolling, nothing else matters.

✅ Good: "This one mistake is killing your LinkedIn engagement."

❌ Bad: "Here are some thoughts on LinkedIn posting strategies…"

2. Your formatting is bad

No one reads walls of text. Structure your posts so they’re easy to skim.

✅ Good: Short paragraphs, spacing, and lists

❌ Bad: One giant block of text

3. You aren’t replying to comments

Engagement drives visibility. If people comment and you don’t respond, you’re killing your reach.

✅ Good: Jump into the comments, ask follow-ups, keep the conversation going

❌ Bad: Post and disappear

4. Your CTA isn’t strong enough

If you don’t tell people what to do next, they won’t do anything.

✅ Good: "Drop a comment if this has happened to you."

❌ Bad: No CTA, or something vague like "Thoughts?"

5. You post and ghost

LinkedIn pushes posts that get engagement early. If you aren’t active before and after posting, your reach will tank.

✅ Good: Engage with other posts before you publish, then stick around for the first 30 minutes

❌ Bad: Post, close LinkedIn, and come back three hours later

Save this so you can troubleshoot your next post.

1/ AI agents fail when they can't access the right data at the right time. The winners connect to existing workflows - calendar, email, and most importantly, meetings.

2/ Companies don't want "general" AI. They want agents that solve specific problems really well. The best performing ones focus on single use cases like sales coaching or customer support QA.

3/ Integration > Innovation. Enterprises care more about how an agent fits into their tech stack than how "cutting edge" the AI is.

4/ Security is non-negotiable. The companies seeing actual adoption? They let IT teams control data access and retention at a granular level.

The winners aren’t just building cool tech. They’re solving real workflow problems.

content:
Don't blunder when pricing AI features. Here's what we've learned from our customers' approaches.

As AI reshapes how we work, the old “per seat, per month” pricing model doesn’t always capture the value that AI adds. Companies are trying new approaches, but each comes with trade-offs:

1️⃣ Per-user add-ons
Notion’s AI add-on costs an extra $10 per user per month. It’s straightforward. But if some users rely on AI features heavily while others barely use it, this can feel awkward fast.

2️⃣ All-in bundling
Grain gives it to everyone. No extra fees and everyone gets the AI features by default. It’s super simple, but if only half your users actually need the features, you might be over-delivering.

3️⃣ Usage-based pricing
Another route is to charge based on how much AI “work” gets done. Think OpenAI’s API charges developers based on tokens consumed. The costs scale with value, but bills become unpredictable. Customers might hesitate if they can’t forecast expenses.

4️⃣ Outcome-based models
Or tie the price directly to results like closed deals or candidates sourced. You pay for what you get, but tracking outcomes can get messy and lead to debates about what’s driving success.

There’s no one “right” way yet. You might mix approaches or experiment until you find what resonates. As AI matures, pricing becomes less about covering costs and more about reflecting real, measurable value.

I took my startup from $0 to multi-million ARR within 18 months. 

One of the biggest lessons I learned: not every dollar of revenue is equally valuable. 

Here's why:

Early-stage startups aren't valued by assets or revenue—they’re valued by potential.

The formula is simple:

Value = P(success) × Payoff + Progress

If a startup manages to piece together $1M in one-off consulting revenue, that still isn't much signal for their potential for success, and won't increase the value of the company.

On the other hand, if a startup hits $1M of revenue from enterprises signing annual contracts, that's a strong sign they've found a big opportunity. 

It's not just about revenue. It's about proving you're likely to succeed. The quality of your traction matters more than the dollar amount 💰

content:
At Recall.ai, we found PMF and grew to multi-million ARR in under a year by ignoring the #1 most common piece of startup advice:

"Launch quickly and iterate using customer feedback"

At my previous startup, I tried to follow that advice, but very quickly learned the uncomfortable truth.

Customer feedback is extremely noisy, and if you're going zero to one, it's virtually useless for telling you what to build.

When I launched that previous product, we had hundreds of users within a month. On the surface, it seemed like a gold-mine of product insight, but they all wanted us to build different things.

I was getting pulled in dozens of different directions, and the product ended up as a Frankenstein of random users' feature requests.

When I started Recall.ai, I decided to do things differently:

1. I started with a strong thesis around what product I should build
2. I built a product which I knew from experience would solve the problem well
3. I used customer feedback to validate and refine my thesis, not to define it

Because we had a clear idea of what we were trying to build and why, we were able to cut through the noise and find the signal from every piece of feedback.

content:
One of the biggest traps early-stage startups fall into is relying on A/B testing. 

Here's why:

When you A/B test, you're only asking one question: "Was this change good?" 

But early on, your product probably has a dozen things wrong with it, and tweaking one variable isn't going to solve that.

The real insights come from talking to your users. A/B testing tells you "yes" or "no" about one small thing. But your users can tell you a hundred things you didn't even think to ask. 

And at this stage, that's what you need: feedback that builds your intuition about the market, not just a tiny bump in a metric.

Don't hide behind statistics. Talk to your users, and really understand what they need.

content:
2 years ago, I was stuck in pivot-hell. Today, I run a multi-million ARR startup. 
The biggest lesson: Building a startup is surprisingly similar to one of the fundamental algorithms in AI — Gradient Descent.

-----

Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm to iteratively find the lowest point in a graph. 

Imagine standing on a hill, and taking successive steps downhill until you can’t go any lower. 

This is how many startup founders approach building their product. They start off with an idea, talk to a few users, build what users ask for, and repeat. 

But there’s a problem with this approach. 

When AI researchers apply gradient descent, a common problem is getting stuck in a local minimum — an area of the graph that’s lower than its surroundings, but far from the best possible result. 

-----

This exact same phenomenon happens with founders building products. 

The first version of the product you build is probably fundamentally broken in several ways, and taking small steps to optimize it won’t bring you to PMF. 

The only way to get out of a local minimum is to take bigger steps. 

This makes taking bigger swings, making larger product changes, or pivoting the business — all strategies where you need to have deep conviction and a detailed understanding of your problem space. 

-----

That’s why it’s so important to build in a space you have deep knowledge of. 
You can’t iterate to success if you’re only taking small steps.

today we launched Day.ai and announced our $4M seed round led by Sequoia.

i’m pumped to talk more about how we’re building Day.ai, but for today i’ll stick why we decided to build it in the first place. we’re on a mission to reimagine CRM for the AI age.

i’ve worked on multiple CRM products in my career, and the fundamental frustration for me was always the same: customers found all of it hard to use, and there was absolutely nothing i could do about it. as somebody who loves great software, that drove me mad.

we’ve forced folks trying to run their business to learn how to become database administrators, schema modelers, and data quality experts. it was the best we could do with the technology we had.

LLMs opened a window of opportunity to actually solve that problem *for real*. instead of teaching people to build a database from their conversations, then query the database to build whatever output they actually want, we can skip the steps in the middle entirely.

i believe productivity software has a special power to unlock great things for humanity when done right. in my view CRM is productivity software that has a huge real-world impact on commerce and how people make a living that ripples out to all of us. can’t wait to see how big of a dent we can make in the problem for the people we serve.

content:
My last startup failed. My current startup found PMF in under 3 months.

The most important lesson I learned about PMF:

Finding PMF isn’t about just solving a valuable problem.

It’s about being the #1 solution for a certain customer, for a certain problem. 

-----

Think about it from the customer’s perspective.

If you have a problem, of course you’re going to want the best solution.

It doesn’t make sense to buy the 2nd best or 3rd best, you always want the #1 product in the market.

-----

But what this means, is if you’re not #1 in your market, it doesn’t make any sense for customers to buy your product. 

And you’ll have a very hard time finding PMF.

-----

The good news is that there’s a straightforward solution.

1) Figure out the customer segment you’re confident you can build the #1 solution for. This could be based off of company size, industry, geography, or more.

2) Build your product so it serves the needs of these customers better than anyone on the market. You should be the no-brainer choice for all of these companies.

3) Once you’ve won your initial market, expand to a slightly bigger customer segment, and win that market as well.

It’s the same playbook startups have used over and over again to topple incumbents.

-----

content:
I’ve pitched over 250 VCs for my last few startups.

One of the most frequent questions I get asked:

“Why is now the right time to start this company?”

Here’s why every top VC asks this question:

The fastest growing companies solve “hair on fire problems”. 
These are problems that are so painful that it’s like having your hair on fire.

Imagine someone with their hair on fire. 
They’re either going to put the fire out, or they’ll die. 
Nobody has their hair on fire for 10 years.

-----

This means if your product could have succeeded 10 years ago, it probably doesn't solve a hair on fire problem.

Burning problems don’t last forever, and windows of opportunities are narrow.

So it’s critically important to understand why your timing makes sense.

-----

content:
My first startup failed. 
My second found PMF in under a year.

This is one of the most important lessons I learned.

Getting feedback from your users is critical. But you can’t rely on feedback to determine your direction.

Here’s an analogy:

Imagine being in a dark maze, searching for the way out.
Your hands can feel around you and tell you what’s nearby.
But your hands can’t tell you where you should go next. You’ve got to have a plan.

This is exactly like user feedback.

Users will tell you if they like the product, and what new features they want but it’s your job to deeply understand:

1. Does my user care about getting their problem solved?
2. Is my product actually solving the problem effectively?
3. Are these the right users I should be serving?
4. Is my product the #1 choice for my users, or do they actually prefer an alternative?

Definitely listen to your users. But it’s your job to figure out what to do.

-----

My first startup never made it past $60k ARR. 
 
My second startup went from 0 to 1M ARR in less than 12 months. 
 
What changed? 
 
First startup: 
 
- Tackled a problem in an industry we didn’t have experience in. 
- Scared of selling. We burned time perfecting the product instead. 
- Paid more attention to competitors instead of customers. 
- Tried to cater to everyone, ended up attracting no one. 
 
Second startup: 
 
- Solving a problem we have domain expertise in. 
- Started selling before we wrote our first line of code. 
- Only serve people within our ICP. Disqualify ruthlessly. 
- Customer obsession. We moved from Canada to the US just to be closer to our customers. 
 
Takeaway: Startups have a limited set of resources. Focus on a small slice of the market that you can feasibly win, then move fast to prove or disprove your hypothesis.

I've closed $1M doing founder-led sales in less than a year.  
I have no sales background, and never understood how to do discovery. 
 
Until this mindset shift: 
 
Instead of trying to “qualify” prospects, you should actively try to disqualify prospects. 
 
----- 
 
Ask scary questions that lead prospects away from your product, such as: 
 
▶️ Why don’t existing solutions such as X, Y and Z work for you? 
 
▶️ Why are you taking time out of your day to chat with me? 
 
▶️  Is this something you need right now, or are you just window shopping? 
 
----- 
 
It’s not the standard way to do discovery, but it: 
 
▶️ Helped us understand why people bought and why people didn’t. 
 
▶️ Maximized our learning per conversation, which is more valuable than revenue when you’re early-stage. 
 
▶️ Helped us find early users with a burning pain. People would self-select out if the pain wasn’t strong enough. 
 
----- 
 
Don't worry about losing prospects. 
 
If your product is valuable, you’ll have hundreds of thousands of potential customers. 
 
If it’s not, it’s better to know sooner rather than later.

content:
I used to think PMF was magic, until we found it at Recall.
It turns out, PMF is actually very simple if you approach it the right way.

Here’s the playbook we followed to find it 👇

There are only 2 components of PMF:

1. Your product: It needs to solve a real problem.
2. Your GTM: It needs to consistently find people with that problem.

Finding PMF is hard when you’re trying to figure out both simultaneously.
You don’t know if your product is the issue, or if you’re talking to the wrong people.

----------

The cheat code is to solve product first, then GTM. And that requires starting with a problem you’re deeply familiar with.

In our case:

1. We targeted a problem we experienced for years. We knew from day 1 who our customers were, and that our product solved a burning pain they had.

2. Next, we iterated on our GTM until we could consistently reach our target customer.

3. Finally, the only thing left to do was reliably close customers and retain them. We fine-tuned product until it clicked.

----------

It’s hard to solve product and GTM at the same time, because if either of them are off, prospects won’t buy and you won’t know why.

But if you know the problem really well, and you’re confident your product solves it, then it’s just about iterating your GTM to find your ideal customer reliably.

This new collaboration will make it easier than ever to build the next generation tools that analyze voice and video.
